notes:
TIME: 0.25 minutes

PURPOSE OF THIS LESSON
Launch the phenomenon and record starting ideas, not a cellular explanation. Read the entire 12-lesson source set before teaching. Cell theory belongs to Lesson 2; organelle functions to Lessons 4–5; specialised wound-healing roles are developed later.

BEFORE CLASS
Prepare a poster with What do we notice? and What do we wonder? Cover the formal driving question until slide 19. Provide one yellow and one blue note per pupil, notebooks, writing materials and a visible timer. If sticky notes are unavailable, use paper slips and tape. Have the Summary Table ready. The four finger drawings are illustrative; no injury demonstration or practical is used.

DO
Use Presenter View. Keep slides 2–3 hidden. Spend 15 seconds introducing the title; the full opening is included in the 5-minute Predict budget. Do not show or preview cell anatomy resources today.

SAY
Today we begin an investigation. Your own ideas and questions are our starting point.

IF…
If projection is unavailable, narrate the story and read the picture descriptions from slides 9–12. No online resource is required.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
The story illustrates a sequence, not a guaranteed healing schedule. Do not infer microscopic causes from these drawings. This is a review draft; native PowerPoint, teacher approval and Calibri fidelity remain unchecked.

TIME: 0 minutes

DO
TEACHER ONLY — HIDDEN SLIDE
HOW TO USE THE NOTES
Every slide has notes written for you, in the same order:
• TIME — how long to spend.
• DO — what to do, step by step.
• SAY — words you can read aloud. Change them to suit your class.
• WAIT TIME — how long to stay silent after a question.
• LOOK FOR — what to listen and look for. This is your formative assessment.
• IF… — what to do when students are stuck or something goes wrong.
• WHY THIS WORKS — the reason behind the strategy, so you can use it in other lessons too.
Tip: In PowerPoint, use Presenter View (Slide Show → Use Presenter View) so you can read these notes while students see only the slide.

ANSWER KEY
A prediction is an initial idea; an observation describes what is seen or described in the evidence; a model represents current thinking. These process definitions do not reveal the unit's biological explanation.

TIME: 0 minutes

DO
Prepare all materials before pupils arrive. Timing: Predict including opening 5 min; Observe 10 min; Explain 7 min; Driving Question Board 10 min; Model Building 5 min; Summary Table 3 min. Total 40 min. Slides 2 and 3 have zero teaching time.

SAY
No new biological content is to be delivered today. Do not show cell labels, cell theory or wound-healing mechanisms.

IF…
No projector: narrate each stage and ask pupils to record the changes they hear. No sticky notes: use paper and tape. Do not replace the lesson with an unpreviewed video.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
Resource audit (names and URLs copied from V2; local availability and actual content have not been verified):
• Wound Healing Process (PLIX), CK-12 — Preview first, not an exact teaching match. Teacher preparation only today: it may disclose mechanisms before pupils investigate.
• Organization in the human body, Khan Academy — Do not use in Lesson 1; it moves to organisation before the launch inquiry.
• Cell parts and their functions; Cell structures and their functions; Comparing animal and plant cells; Plant vs animal cells; Overview of animal and plant cells; Apply: cell parts and functions — Do not use today; these reveal later content. Reconsider during preparation of the relevant later lesson, after previewing.
The three buttons retain the source ARES URLs. No link has been invented or presented as tested.

TIME: 0.5 minutes

DO
• Show the 12 circles. Tell students this is the journey for the next few weeks.
• Do not read the driving question aloud yet. You will reveal it on the Question Board later in the lesson. If students ask, say: “Hold that thought — we will come back to it.”

SAY
• “Over the next 12 lessons we are going to solve a puzzle about our own bodies. Today is lesson 1. Today we ask questions. We do not answer them yet.”

IF…
If pupils read ahead, say: Keep that question. We will reveal our shared question after your own notice and wonder notes.

WHY THIS WORKS
• Students learn better when they know where a lesson fits. A unit map gives them the big picture before the details.

TIME: 0.5 minutes

DO
• Read the three goals aloud.

SAY
• “Today, nobody can be wrong. I want your honest ideas, not the ‘right answer’.”
Observe means describe what you notice. Predict means give your starting idea. A model is a drawing of your current thinking.

WHY THIS WORKS
• Saying “no wrong answers” out loud makes it safe for students to share half-formed ideas. You need those ideas to see what they already think.

PREDICT PHASE (5 minutes total, including title, map and goals)
TIME: 1.25 minutes

DO
• Ask students to close their eyes.
• Read the story below slowly, with feeling. Pause at each full stop.

SAY
• “Amina is in the kitchen in Eastleigh, helping her mother prepare supper. She is slicing onions — the smell is sharp, her eyes are beginning to water. Then the knife slips. She looks down and sees a thin line of red appear on her fingertip. She presses it with her thumb. After about a minute, the bleeding is already slowing down. A dark, sticky material begins to form… What is happening inside that finger right now?”

IF…
If the injury story is uncomfortable, pupils may keep their eyes open or look away and listen. Use the non-graphic drawings; do not use injury photographs.

WHY THIS WORKS
• A story about an everyday event in a familiar place makes the science feel real. Closing eyes helps students picture it and focus.

TIME: 2.5 minutes

DO
• Students open their eyes and write.
• Start a 2-minute timer. Stay silent. Walk slowly between the rows.
• Read over shoulders WITHOUT commenting.

SAY
• “I want everyone to write in your notebook. Do not talk yet. Do not look at your neighbour. Just write what you think. You have 2 full minutes.”

WAIT TIME
• The full 2 minutes. Do not hint or prompt. Your silence tells students that thinking time is real.

LOOK FOR
• What range of ideas do students have? Do they mention blood clotting, skin repair, germs/bacteria, or specific cells (platelets, white blood cells)?
• Or do they only describe the outside of the wound (“it bleeds, then it stops”)?
• Make a mental note. You will use it to guide the class discussion.

IF…
If a pupil cannot begin, preserve the silent writing period. Note the blank response for later support; do not supply a cell name or mechanism.

WHY THIS WORKS
• Writing BEFORE talking means every student has their own idea — not just the confident ones. These notebook entries are their starting point. In Lesson 12 they will compare them with what they finally understand.

ANSWER KEY
No single correct biological response is expected. Preserve each pupil’s own initial idea, uncorrected, for comparison in Lesson 12.

OBSERVE PHASE (10 minutes total)
TIME: 2 minutes

DO
• Pairs share their written predictions for 90 seconds.
• Circulate and listen. Note one or two interesting or surprising ideas to call on later.

SAY
• “Turn to your partner. Read what you wrote. Find one thing that is the same and one thing that is different. You have 90 seconds.”

IF…
If only one partner speaks, ask the quieter partner to read their own written prediction. Keep the full 90-second sharing window.

WHY THIS WORKS
• Talking in pairs before the whole class lets quieter students rehearse their ideas in a safe space.

ANSWER KEY
Pairs report a similarity and a difference between their own predictions; no mechanism is confirmed.

TIME: 1 minutes

DO
• Show one picture at a time. Each click adds the next picture.
• For each picture, ask “What do you notice?” then wait.
• Students add anything new to their notebook prediction.
• No projector? Read the picture description below aloud instead.

SAY
• “Look carefully. What do you notice?”

WAIT TIME
• 5 full seconds after you ask, before you take any answer. Observation needs thinking time.
PICTURE 1 (read aloud if needed): A fresh cut across the fingertip. A line of red blood, with drops running down.

LOOK FOR
Pupils describe the red line and blood from the narrated drawing, rather than naming an unseen mechanism. Read at least four notebook additions across the sequence.

ANSWER KEY
The source sequence is: blood appears; bleeding slows and a clot forms; a scab develops; new skin appears over several days. Accept only the stage already revealed. These are illustrative observations, not a microscopic explanation.

TIME: 1 minutes

DO
• Click to show the next picture. Ask: “What changed between this picture and the last one?”

SAY
• “What changed between picture 1 and picture 2?”

WAIT TIME
• 5 full seconds after you ask, before you take any answer. Observation needs thinking time.
PICTURE 2 (read aloud if needed): The bleeding has stopped. A dark red, sticky clot fills the cut.

LOOK FOR
Pupils distinguish the visible slowing of bleeding/darker material from an explanation of why it happens.

ANSWER KEY
The source sequence is: blood appears; bleeding slows and a clot forms; a scab develops; new skin appears over several days. Accept only the stage already revealed. These are illustrative observations, not a microscopic explanation.

TIME: 1 minutes

DO
• Click to show the next picture. Ask: “What changed between this picture and the last one?”

SAY
• “What changed between picture 2 and picture 3?”

WAIT TIME
• 5 full seconds after you ask, before you take any answer. Observation needs thinking time.
PICTURE 3 (read aloud if needed): The clot has dried into a hard, dark brown scab.

LOOK FOR
Pupils compare the new visible scab with the earlier appearance. They should not copy a future panel caption.

ANSWER KEY
The source sequence is: blood appears; bleeding slows and a clot forms; a scab develops; new skin appears over several days. Accept only the stage already revealed. These are illustrative observations, not a microscopic explanation.

TIME: 2 minutes

DO
• Click to show the next picture. Ask: “What changed between this picture and the last one?”

SAY
• “What changed between picture 3 and picture 4?”

WAIT TIME
• 5 full seconds after you ask, before you take any answer. Observation needs thinking time.

LOOK FOR
• Has any student mentioned cells (platelets, white blood cells, skin cells)? If yes, note the name — this is a bridge to Lesson 8.
• If nobody talks about cells, that is expected. It confirms why we need this unit.

IF…
If a pupil names a cell type, record it as their idea without confirming it. Say: We will test that idea in later lessons.

WHY THIS WORKS
• Showing the pictures one at a time slows students down and makes them compare. Comparing “before” and “after” is a core science skill.
PICTURE 4 (read aloud if needed): The scab has fallen off. Only a faint pink line of new skin is left.

ANSWER KEY
The source sequence is: blood appears; bleeding slows and a clot forms; a scab develops; new skin appears over several days. Accept only the stage already revealed. These are illustrative observations, not a microscopic explanation.

TIME: 3 minutes

DO
• Ask 3–4 pairs to share. Choose students who do not usually raise their hand.
• Write their key phrases on the board WORD FOR WORD. For example: “the blood goes hard”, “white cells come”, “skin grows back”.
• Do not correct or praise any idea yet. Keep this list — you will use it later in the unit.

SAY
• “I am writing your ideas exactly as you said them. I am not telling you yet whether they are right or not. Every idea here is valuable data — it tells us what we already know and what we still need to find out.”

LOOK FOR
• This board list is your map of what the class already knows. Note which ideas are common and which are rare.

IF…
If pupils look to you for a verdict, say: I am recording your words. We will investigate which explanations the evidence supports.

WHY THIS WORKS
• Recording ideas without judging them is what scientists do: observe first, interpret later. It also makes students feel safe to share ideas they are unsure about.

EXPLAIN PHASE (7 minutes total)
TIME: 1.5 minutes

DO
• Ask the question. Wait. Take 2–3 answers.
• Reply to each answer with another question — do NOT say “right” or “wrong”.

SAY
• If a student says “the blood goes hard”: “Interesting — what do you think makes it go hard? Is that a chemical change? A physical change? Something else?”

WAIT TIME
• 5 seconds before taking answers.

LOOK FOR
Listen for causal suggestions, keeping these tentative. No pupil is required to provide the later cellular explanation.

WHY THIS WORKS
• These questions move students from describing (“the bleeding slows”) to asking about causes (“what makes it slow?”). Answering with a question keeps students thinking instead of waiting for you to give the answer. This is called Socratic questioning.

TIME: 1.5 minutes

DO
• Ask the question. Wait. Take 2–3 answers.
• Keep probing: “Why do you think that?”

WAIT TIME
• 5 seconds before taking answers.

LOOK FOR
• Can students imagine MANY things working at once, or only one cause? Students who describe several processes without being prompted are ready for the idea of cell specialisation.

IF…
If pupils offer only one cause, use the source follow-up: Why do you think that? Do not teach the separate cell roles.

TIME: 2 minutes

DO
• Show the 10-second timer. Count silently to 10. Do not rephrase the question.
• Take 2–3 answers.

WAIT TIME
• A FULL 10 seconds — this is the hardest question. Resist the urge to help. Silence is harder for the teacher than for the students.

LOOK FOR
• Listen for students who say “they would look different” and can give a reason.

IF…
• If nobody answers after 10 seconds: “Talk to your partner for 30 seconds, then I will ask again.”

WHY THIS WORKS
The question moves from cause to the possibility of several structures doing different jobs; it does not establish their identities.

TIME: 2 minutes

DO
• Read the statement slowly. This is a “bridging statement”: it is NOT an answer. It sets up the big question.
• Pause. Then ask: “Does that surprise you? Why?” Take 2–3 answers.

SAY
• “That raises a very big question, which we are going to investigate for the next several weeks.”

WHY THIS WORKS
• The statement creates a puzzle: if so many different structures are at work, why do they look different? A puzzle makes students want to find out. Do not name the cells yet — that comes in Lesson 8.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
This is the source bridging statement. Do not name platelets, neutrophils, macrophages or fibroblasts unless recording a pupil’s own prior idea; do not confirm their roles today.

DRIVING QUESTION BOARD (10 minutes total)
TIME: 7 minutes

DO
• Model first: read the two example notes on the slide as YOUR notes (“think aloud”).
• Give each student one yellow and one blue sticky note. 3 minutes to write.
• Students come up in groups of 6–8 and post notes under the two columns.
• Read some “wonder” questions aloud. Group similar ones together on the poster.

SAY
• “I notice in the pictures that the wound looks completely healed after just a few days — that is my notice note. I wonder how the body knows exactly what shape to rebuild the skin in — that is my wonder note.”
• “Your wonder note should be a real question you actually have — not a question you think I want to hear.”
• After posting: “Every single question on this board is legitimate. Some we will answer in this unit. Some might take years of science to answer. All of them matter.”

LOOK FOR
Check that each pupil produces one observation and one genuine question. Use the actual healing sequence as the observation source, not a textbook mechanism.

IF…
If pupils write what they think you want, repeat the source prompt: Your wonder note should be a real question you actually have.

WHY THIS WORKS
• Separating “notice” (observation) from “wonder” (question) teaches a basic science skill. When students see their own questions on the board, they own the investigation. Modelling the task first shows students exactly what a good note looks like.

ANSWER KEY
A notice refers to an appearance or change in the sequence. A wonder is the pupil’s own open question; there is no single correct question.

TIME: 3 minutes

DO
• Uncover the driving question at the top of the poster. Read it aloud slowly.
• Wait 8 seconds in silence. Then ask: “What is your very first reaction to this question?” Take 2–3 answers.
• Explain that this question will be answered piece by piece, and the board will be updated at the end of every lesson.
• After class: photograph the board.

WAIT TIME
• 8 seconds after reading the question.

LOOK FOR
• After class, sort the “wonder” notes into: (a) questions this unit will answer, (b) questions that show a misconception, (c) questions that show sophisticated thinking. Use this to plan Lessons 2–5.

IF…
If a note is an explanation presented as an observation, ask: Which change did you actually see or hear described? Keep the proposed cause as an idea to investigate.

WHY THIS WORKS
• The driving question comes AFTER students post their own questions, so they can see their questions connect to it. It feels like THEIR investigation, not the teacher’s.

ANSWER KEY
There is no required first reaction. Record the actual questions; do not supply a unit answer.

MODEL BUILDING PHASE (5 minutes total)
TIME: 5 minutes

DO
• Give NO diagrams or books. Students draw only from what they already know.
• Give a full 3 minutes. Show the timer.
• Circulate. Ask individual students: “What made you draw it that way?” or “What is this part doing?” Do not correct any drawing.

SAY
• “This is not an art competition and it is not a test. It is a snapshot of what you already know. Draw whatever comes to mind — a box, a circle, dots inside, labels — anything at all.”

LOOK FOR
• After class, look at the drawings (or photograph a few). Common patterns:
• a circle with nothing inside;
• a circle with only a nucleus;
• several named parts (some prior learning);
• cells drawn as bricks or boxes (because of the word “cell”).
• Use these patterns to plan Lesson 2.

IF…
If a pupil asks for a cell diagram, say: Draw whatever comes to mind. This records your starting idea, not a correct-answer test.

WHY THIS WORKS
• This drawing is the baseline. Students will revise their model in nearly every lesson. Seeing how their own drawing changes shows them that learning is revision — being wrong at the start is normal.

ANSWER KEY
There is no correct baseline cell drawing. Accept the pupil’s own sketch and any labels they already know. Do not show an exemplar. Compare with later revisions.

TIME: 3 minutes

DO
• Students start the first row of their Summary Table. They finish it at home.
• Close by returning to Amina. Say the closing line slowly. Pause after the word “predictions”.

SAY
• “In Lesson 2, we will begin to look at what a cell actually is. But today, you have already done something scientists do every time they start an investigation — you observed carefully, asked good questions, and made your first predictions. Hold onto those predictions. We will need them again.”

IF…
If the explanation column is blank, prompt: What can we explain yet, and what are we still wondering? The source explicitly accepts that the cellular explanation is still unknown.

ANSWER KEY
• Observe: When a finger is cut, the bleeding slows, a clot forms, a scab develops, and new skin appears over several days.
• Learn: This familiar process is made up of many events happening at the same time. Scientists have found many different types of tiny structures working together during healing.
• Explain: We cannot yet explain why the structures look different or how each one knows its job. Our Driving Question Board will help us answer that over the next eleven lessons.

TEACHER REFLECTION
• Did students write real “wonder” questions, or what they thought you wanted?
• Were students willing to share incomplete ideas? If not, what held them back?
• Did you really wait 8–10 seconds after the hardest questions?
• Did anyone already mention platelets or white blood cells? Plan how to use that knowledge later without making others feel behind.
• Are the wonder questions rich enough to drive 12 lessons, or do you need to add a few of your own in Lesson 2?
